explanations.explanation: Ezekiel says it plainly: he saw a great many bones on the valley floor, "…and indeed, they were very dry." (Ezekiel 37:2) The LORD led him all around among them, so he got a close look. Hold onto that picture, because it matters for what comes next.

Warm isn't the word the text uses. Ezekiel sees bones on the valley floor, and the text says they were "very dry." (Ezekiel 37:2) Dry is the word, and it sets the stage for what the LORD is about to do.
Stacked isn't what the text pictures, friend. Ezekiel is led all around among the bones on the floor of the valley. What the text tells us about them is that they were "very dry." (Ezekiel 37:2)

explanations.answer: Can these bones come to life
explanations.explanation: That's the question. The LORD asks, "Son of man, can these bones come to life?" (Ezekiel 37:3) "Son of man…" is how He addresses Ezekiel here. Of all the things He could ask in a valley full of dry bones, He asks that one. It sets up the whole scene.

Good detective thinking, but the LORD doesn't ask who they were. He asks Ezekiel, "Son of man, can these bones come to life?" (Ezekiel 37:3) The question isn't about the past at all. It points straight at what could happen next.

explanations.answer: How long have these been here
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd guess that. Dry bones look like they've been sitting a while. But the LORD never asks about time. He asks Ezekiel, "Son of man, can these bones come to life?" (Ezekiel 37:3) That question looks forward, not back.

Ezekiel doesn't say that. When the LORD asks if the bones can come to life, he answers, "O Lord GOD, only You know." (Ezekiel 37:3) That's not a no. He leaves the answer in God's hands, which is a pretty good place to leave it.

Right, Ezekiel never says it could never happen. He replies, "O Lord GOD, only You know." (Ezekiel 37:3) No yes, no no, just handing the question back to the One who can answer it. Honestly, I'd have blurted out something way less wise.

Breath it is. The Lord GOD says, "I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life." (Ezekiel 37:5) Notice who's doing the work: He says "I will." The bones don't have to do a thing but listen.
Water makes sense for dry bones, friend. Dry, water, easy. But the Lord GOD says, "I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life." (Ezekiel 37:5) Breath is what He promises, not water.

Fire is a big one, and I respect the drama. I know a thing or two about what fire does to a cookie. But here the Lord GOD says, "I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life." (Ezekiel 37:5) No fire in the promise, just breath.

That's the finish line of the promise. After the tendons, flesh, skin and breath, God says, "Then you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 37:6) The whole thing ends with them knowing who He is. Not a bad takeaway from a valley of bones.

Ezekiel is doing the talking, so I see the guess. But God's words to the bones end somewhere else: "Then you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 37:6) The focus is on who God is, not on who's speaking.

That's a big and beautiful thing, but it's not what God says here. His words to the bones finish with, "Then you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 37:6) He doesn't mention sins in this promise. Stick with what the verse gives us.

A rattling! Ezekiel says, "…there was suddenly a noise, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to bone." (Ezekiel 37:7) Picture a whole valley of bones clacking into place. That's one sound I'd stop everything to hear.
A trumpet would be a grand entrance, I'll give you that. But Ezekiel hears "…a noise, a rattling…" (Ezekiel 37:7) It's the sound of bones coming together, not a horn.
A shout feels natural for a moment this big, friend. But the text says there was suddenly "…a noise, a rattling…" (Ezekiel 37:7) The rattling is the bones themselves coming together, bone to bone.
True. Ezekiel says the bones "…came together, bone to bone." (Ezekiel 37:7) This happens as he prophesies, just as he was commanded. The valley goes from scattered bones to bones joined up.

Actually it's true. Ezekiel says that as he prophesied, there was a rattling, "…and the bones came together, bone to bone." (Ezekiel 37:7) The bones don't stay scattered. They come together right as he speaks.

Not yet, friend. The text says tendons appeared, flesh grew and skin covered them, "but there was no breath in them." (Ezekiel 37:8) They look like bodies, but they aren't breathing. The story has one more step to go.
Right. Ezekiel sees tendons, flesh and skin, "but there was no breath in them." (Ezekiel 37:8) So they have the look of bodies, but no breathing yet. That missing breath is the detail to hold onto.

The four winds. God tells Ezekiel to say, "Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain, so that they may live!" (Ezekiel 37:9) That's breath called in from every direction. Nobody's left out of the call.
Mountains are a fun guess, since breath and wind feel like they'd come from up high. But God says, "Come from the four winds, O breath…" (Ezekiel 37:9) The winds are the source, not the mountains.
Deep sea, that's a bold guess! But no sea in this verse. God tells Ezekiel to say, "Come from the four winds, O breath…" (Ezekiel 37:9) The four winds are where He calls the breath from.
True. Ezekiel says, "…the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet…" (Ezekiel 37:10) The bodies that were lying still are up and standing. The breath was the missing piece.

It's actually true, friend. Ezekiel says, "…the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet…" (Ezekiel 37:10) The breath comes in, and they're up. Just what God said would happen.
A vast army. Ezekiel says they came to life and stood on their feet, "…a vast army." (Ezekiel 37:10) The valley had been full of bones. Now it's a whole army standing up.
A choir would sound lovely, but that's not the word Ezekiel uses. He says they stood on their feet, "…a vast army." (Ezekiel 37:10) An army, friend, not a choir.
A family is a warm thought, and I'm partial to the idea. But Ezekiel says they stood on their feet, "…a vast army." (Ezekiel 37:10) That's the word the text gives.

Their hope. The people say, "Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off." (Ezekiel 37:11) Those are heavy words. I think that's a hard place to be, and God doesn't skip over it. He takes their own words and answers them.

Harvest is a reasonable guess, but it's not in their words. The people say, "Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off." (Ezekiel 37:11) It's hope that they say is gone. That's a different kind of loss.
Homes feel like they'd fit, friend. But the people say, "Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off." (Ezekiel 37:11) What they say has perished is their hope.

Their graves. God says, "O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them…" (Ezekiel 37:12) He says "My people," so these are His own. Opening graves is a big promise, and He says it again in verse 13.
City gates are a good guess, but that's not what God opens. He says, "…I will open your graves and bring you up from them…" (Ezekiel 37:12) It's graves He promises to open.

Prison doors fit the feeling of being stuck, I'll admit, and I know a little about being shut in a drawer. But God says, "…I will open your graves and bring you up from them…" (Ezekiel 37:12) Graves are what He names.
True. God says, "…I will bring you back to the land of Israel." (Ezekiel 37:12) That promise comes right alongside opening the graves. He's not just lifting them up, He's bringing them home.
It's actually true, friend. In the same breath as opening the graves, God says, "…I will bring you back to the land of Israel." (Ezekiel 37:12) Both promises are right there in the verse.
Spirit. God says, "I will put My Spirit in you and you will live…" (Ezekiel 37:14) The same verse says He'll settle them in their own land. That's a promise straight from His own mouth.
Law is a good Bible word, and I see why it came to mind. But in this verse God says, "I will put My Spirit in you and you will live…" (Ezekiel 37:14) It's His Spirit He promises to put in them.
Strength sounds right for a vast army that just stood on its feet. But the verse says, "I will put My Spirit in you and you will live…" (Ezekiel 37:14) God names His Spirit, not strength.

No open question here, friend. God says, "Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD." (Ezekiel 37:14) He says He has spoken, and He adds "…I will do it…" Nothing is left hanging.

Right, nothing left open. God says, "Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD." (Ezekiel 37:14) He doesn't just speak. He says He will do it, and that's the last word on it.
